description: The migration-safety recall fixture, and the only place any `DJM` rule has a known answer. This family cannot be measured the way the others are, and the reason is worth stating because it drove the family's design. Every `DJM` rule reports on something a migration does at the moment it runs -- a lock it takes, a statement that aborts -- and a migration sitting in a shipped project's history demonstrably ran. So NetBox, pretix and Healthchecks cannot supply a true positive for this family even in principle: reporting across their 875 migrations would have produced roughly 1600 findings whose true-positive rate is zero by construction. That is why the static tier reports only the leaf of each app's history, and why recall has to be measured here instead. The structure carries the argument. `billing` holds the defects and `ledger` holds their correctly-written twins, and each pair differs only in the thing the rule is about: for `DJM-001` a `default` on one side, for `DJM-002` the direction of a `max_length` change -- narrowed on the defect, widened on the control, which Postgres has skipped rewriting since 9.2 -- for `DJM-003` whether the index is built concurrently, the control paying for that with the `atomic = False` the operation requires, for `DJM-004` whether the column is dropped outright or through the `database_operations` half of a `SeparateDatabaseAndState`, and for `DJM-005` whether a renamed column is pinned back into place with `db_column`. The `DJM-004` pair is the sharpest one here, because the replay flattens the wrapper away and the two sides reach the rule as the same bare `RemoveField` -- a rule matching on the operation name alone would report the control, which is to say it would report the fix its own remediation recommends. `DJM-006` differs only in whether the backfill sitting beside all those schema changes carries a reverse, and its control supplies `RunPython.noop` rather than taking the rule's other remediation of moving the data pass into a migration of its own -- a control built that way would be measuring a different fix from the one it is paired against. `DJM-007` is the one pair whose defect is not a schema operation at all but the body of a data migration, and it is deliberately written so that no other rule reports it: the loop accumulates and issues one `bulk_update`, which is `DJP-007`'s remediation carried out in full, and that remediation is what makes the memory worse. Had the fixture also saved inside the loop, both rules would have reported the same line and neither the fixture nor the rule would have shown that this one has a claim of its own. Its control keeps the `bulk_update` and adds `.iterator(chunk_size=500)` plus a per-chunk flush, so the pair differs only in whether the fetch and the list it feeds are bounded. `DJM-008` is the one pair that needed no new operations at all, and that is the point of it: `billing.0002` already ran five schema changes and then a backfill inside one transaction, which is exactly the shape, and `ledger.0002` already carried `atomic = False`. Two rules therefore report line 101 -- `DJM-006` because the backfill has no reverse, `DJM-008` because it runs while five `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` locks are still held -- and that is honest rather than duplicated: the first is about whether a failed deploy can go back, the second about what the table does while the deploy is still going forwards. `ledger`'s `atomic = False` is shared with the `DJM-003` control, which is worth naming because it means one un-fix has to be read as evidence for two rules. This manifest forbids any finding in `ledger` at all rather than at particular lines, because a line-numbered control stops guarding anything the first time someone inserts an operation, and does it silently. Reachability is measured rather than assumed by scripts/fixture_controls_probe.py, which removes the fix from each control and requires the matching rule to then report it -- a control that passes by being unreachable is indistinguishable from a rule that is broken. Both migrations are hand-written, which is not incidental: `makemigrations` prompts for a one-off default and so cannot emit `billing.0002`, and hand-written migrations are precisely what this family targets.
